title: Timeouts, refusals, resets and the diagnostic framework
summary: Every failure has a signature. Learn the signatures, then use the framework rather than a fixed checklist — because real incidents do not cooperate with a linear order.

sections.heading: The six failure signatures
sections.html:
Error you seeWhat happenedWhat it rules out
Name or service not knownResolution failed before any packet was sentEverything about transport, routing and the server
Network unreachableNo route for the destination, from the local kernelFirewall and server
No route to hostICMP destination-unreachable from a router, or ARP failed locallyNothing upstream of that router
Connection refusedTCP RST receivedReachability — the host is up
Connection timed outNo response to SYNThe server has no listener? No — that gives RST. Timeout means drop
Connection reset by peerRST mid-session (firewall state, app crash, idle timeout)Nothing about the initial connectivity

Memorise the mapping from error text to layer. In an interview this is the fastest way to demonstrate that you diagnose rather than guess.

sections.heading: What each layer's failure actually looks like
sections.html:
InterfaceNo carrier, no address, or an address from 169.254. ip link, ip addr.
IP / maskLocal works, remote does not, or ARP failures for addresses that should be remote. ip route, ip neigh.
ARP / NDPNeighbour FAILED, traffic silently dropped. ip neigh, arping.
Routingip route get reveals the wrong next hop; traceroute stops early.
DNSIP literal works, name fails. dig, getent hosts.
FirewallTimeout, not refusal, and only for some ports or sources.
TransportRefused, reset, or half-open sockets in ss.
ApplicationTCP connects but the protocol misbehaves; 500s, TLS errors, wrong content.

sections.heading: The framework, with the flexibility clause
sections.html:
1. Understand the reported symptom precisely. 'The site is down' is not a symptom; 'Chrome shows ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT to wiki for three users since 09:10' is.
  2. Identify scope: one user or all, one site or all, since when, after what change.
  3. Interface and link status.
  4. IP configuration.
  5. Local network and gateway.
  6. Routing.
  7. DNS.
  8. Transport-layer connectivity.
  9. Service listening and logs.
  10. Form a hypothesis, then verify it with evidence that could have falsified it.

The clause: this is a guide, not a law. If the complaint is 'the site loads but says 502', you do not start at the interface — the evidence already tells you transport and DNS work. Good troubleshooters jump to the layer implicated by the error text and only walk forward when they must. What makes the order valuable is that it guarantees you check the cheap things before the expensive ones.

sections.heading: Diagnosing the same incident three ways
sections.html:
Scenario A — 'It is slow.' Loss and jitter (ping, MTR) first; then congestion signals (interface errors, ip -s link, retransmits from ss -ti), then application latency. Note: latency problems are rarely DNS unless the first lookup is slow and cached ones are fast — measurable with dig's timing line.

Scenario B — 'It works from my desk, not from theirs.' Scope and path difference: different VLAN, different resolver, different route. Compare ip route get, resolver config and DNS answers between the two clients.

Scenario C — 'It worked yesterday.' Change analysis beats guessing: recent configuration, certificate expiry, lease expiry, DNS TTL change, routing change, a service restart. Ask what changed before touching anything.

sections.heading: What to say in an interview
sections.html:
A strong answer sounds like: 'First I would scope it and look at the exact error. If it is a name error, I test resolution separately from reachability. If resolution works, I test the port to the resolved IP and read whether it refuses or times out, which tells me whether something is listening or whether a filter is dropping. Then I check the listener and logs on the server. I would also check what changed, because a sudden failure with no previous symptoms is usually a change, not a degradation.'

That answer contains evidence, a hypothesis, and a decision point. It is worth more than a memorised ten-step checklist delivered without reasoning.

checks.prompt: curl hangs for 30 seconds then reports a timeout, but a packet capture shows the SYN leaving the client. Which cause fits best?
options: A firewall or ACL is dropping the SYN, or the server is down
No listener on the destination port
checks.explanation: No listener produces a RST (refused). Silence after a SYN means the packet or its reply is dropped — a filter, or a host that is not responding.

why_wrong.0: The capture proves the address was known and the SYN was sent.
why_wrong.2: TLS happens after a TCP handshake, which never completed.

checks.prompt: Which is the strongest evidence that DNS is working but the application is not?
options: MTR shows loss at an intermediate hop
The name resolves to an IP, connections to the port are refused, and ss shows no listener
checks.explanation: Resolution succeeded, transport reached the host, and the absence of a listener localises the fault to the service.

why_wrong.3: Ping failure proves nothing about DNS.
why_wrong.2: Starred hops usually indicate ICMP filtering.
why_wrong.0: Intermediate loss is often rate limiting; it says nothing about DNS.

checks.prompt: Given only the error text, state the layer and the first command for each of: 'could not resolve host', 'connection refused', 'connection timed out', 'connection reset by peer'.

checklist.text: Could not resolve host: name resolution; test with dig/getent and check nsswitch/hosts/resolv.conf.
Connection refused: transport/listener; test with ss -ltnp on the server and check the bound address.
Connection timed out: filtering or unreachable host; check capture, firewall, routing.
Connection reset by peer: mid-session termination; check firewall state, idle timeouts, application logs.
States clearly that each error text already excludes some layers, which is why the error is the first clue.

checks.reference: Resolution error -> DNS/NSS layer, before any packet: dig, getent hosts, resolv.conf, hosts file. Refused -> RST from a reachable host: ss -ltnp and the bind address. Timed out -> packets dropped: tcpdump, firewall rules, routing. Reset -> an established connection was torn down: firewall state table, idle timeouts, application or proxy behaviour, and server logs. Reading the error text correctly eliminates whole layers at once.

connect.title: DNS module
connect.text: Resolution failures have their own distinct signature; never conflate them with connectivity failures.

connect.title: Process module
connect.text: Once transport reaches the host, ss and systemctl/journalctl own the investigation.

connect.title: All case studies
connect.text: Every mission in this application is graded on whether you identified the layer, not just the answer.

interview.q: What is the difference between connection refused and connection timed out?
interview.a: Refused means a TCP RST arrived: the host is reachable but nothing is listening (or a REJECT rule fired). Timed out means no reply at all: a DROP rule, a dead host, or a black-holed route. The distinction decides whether you look at the listener or at the path.

interview.q: How do you troubleshoot an intermittent problem?
interview.a: Make it measurable: capture or monitor over time, quantify frequency and conditions (time of day, load, source), and correlate with changes. Intermittency usually means multiple paths or servers, resource contention, expiring timers (leases, certificates, TTLs), or packet loss, so instrumenting beats guessing.
